```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4.5
)
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(unimlsurv)
  library(mlr3)
})
```

This vignette walks through every number `unimlsurv` produces, one at a time.
Each section answers the same three questions:

1. **What question does this number answer?** (No formulas.)
2. **How do I read it?** (Good values, bad values, and what moves it.)
3. **When should I not read it?** (Small samples, heavy censoring, horizons
   the data cannot support.)

All examples use one simulated cohort of 300 patients with a **known truth**,
so every number can be compared against the model that generated the data.
The main workflow vignette shows how these pieces assemble into a paper.

```{r data}
data <- sim_surv_data(n = 300, seed = 2026)
time_points <- c(3, 6, 12)
truth <- sim_surv_truth(data, time_points)

## One fitted Cox model for the whole tutorial
spec <- surv_spec(time = "time", status = "status", time_points = time_points)
prepared <- as_surv_data(data, spec)
task <- make_surv_task(prepared, spec)
fitted <- train_surv(task, resolve_surv_learners("coxph", tune = FALSE)$coxph$learner)
prediction <- predict_surv_learner(fitted, prepared$data, time_points)
survival <- survival_matrix(prediction, time_points)
risk <- survival_risk(prediction)
```

## Thirty seconds on censoring

A survival outcome is two columns: how long the patient was observed, and
whether an event happened. A patient who moved away after 8 months is not
"alive at 8 months" and not "dead at 8 months" — the record only says "no event
during the first 8 months". Censored patients still carry information (they
were event-free *up to* their last contact), and every metric in this package
uses that information correctly: either by dropping censored patients from
comparisons they cannot inform, or by re-weighting with the censoring
survival. The package never lets you turn the outcome into a plain 0/1 column.

## Discrimination, part 1: Harrell's C

**Question.** When one patient had the event before another, did the model
rank the sicker one higher?

```{r harrell}
surv_cindex(data$time, data$status, risk)
```

**Reading.** 0.5 is a coin flip; 0.6 is weak; 0.7 is usable; 0.75+ is good for
clinical data. `0` and `1` never appear in real cohorts. Pairs are only
"comparable" when the earlier event tells you the order — censored patients
join a pair only through their event-free stretch.

**Do not read it when.** The censoring distributions of two cohorts differ:
the comparable-pair set then differs too, and the same model earns different
C-indices for reasons unrelated to the model. That is exactly the gap Uno's C
closes, which is why papers report both.

```{r truth-c}
## The truth itself, scored the same way — the ceiling this data allows
surv_cindex(data$time, data$status, truth$risk)
```

The simulated truth earns about `r round(surv_cindex(data$time, data$status,
truth$risk), 2)` on this cohort: that is the ceiling the noise and censoring
impose, and a good model should land close to it.

## Discrimination, part 2: Uno's C

**Question.** The same question, with the censoring dependence removed. Uno's
C (2011) truncates the analysis at a horizon `tau`, weights each event
patient by the inverse **squared** censoring survival estimated on the
**training** data, and discards tied risk scores.

```{r uno-c}
set.seed(7)
index <- sample.int(nrow(data), 150)
surv_cindex_uno(
  time_train = data$time[-index], status_train = data$status[-index],
  time_test = data$time[index], status_test = data$status[index],
  risk_test = risk[index]
)
```

**Reading.** Same scale as Harrell's C. Report the two side by side; when they
disagree, the disagreement is about the censoring, not the model. The training
data are part of the definition — the package refuses to estimate the weights
on the evaluation set, because that is a different (and wrong) censoring
distribution.

**Do not read it when.** Your horizon `tau` runs past the training follow-up:
the censoring survival becomes 0 and patients are dropped, which the
reference implementation also does. Keep `tau` inside the training follow-up.

## Discrimination over time: the time-dependent AUC

**Question.** At a chosen horizon `t`, does the model separate the patients
who had an event by `t` from those still event-free after it? This is the
question a clinician asks at a decision point, and it is *local*: a model can
have an excellent overall C and a poor AUC at your horizon.

```{r tdauc}
metrics <- calc_surv_metrics(
  data$time, data$status, risk, survival, time_points
)
metrics$by_time[, c("time", "n_case", "n_control", "auc", "auc_uno")]
```

**Reading.** Again 0.5 is the coin flip. Watch `n_case` and `n_control`: an
AUC built on 3 cases is noise. The cumulative/dynamic AUC (`auc`) weights its
pairs with the censoring survival estimated on the evaluation data; Uno's
`auc_uno` takes the case weights from the **training** censoring curve. When
they disagree on a small validation set, report both.

The ROC curve behind the number is available too, so the figure and the
quantity cannot disagree:

```{r roc, fig.cap = "Cumulative/dynamic ROC at 6 months."}
curve <- surv_roc_curve(data$time, data$status, survival[, 2], 6)
head(curve, 3)
```

**Do not read it when.** `n_case` or `n_control` is small, or when the horizon
sits past the observed follow-up: the package returns `NA` there instead of a
number nobody can defend.

## Prediction error: Brier score and IBS

**Question.** Is the predicted S(t) close to what actually happened? Unlike
the AUC, this is a proper scoring rule: it can only be improved by predicting
the truth.

```{r brier}
metrics$by_time[, c("time", "brier")]
```

**Reading.** Lower is better; 0.25 is the score of predicting 0.5 for
everyone, and the benchmark curve is the Brier score of the Kaplan-Meier
estimator (the "no model at all" baseline). A model must beat that baseline to
be worth anything. `ibs` integrates the Brier score over your grid and divides
by its width, so it stays on the Brier scale — and it inherits the grid: two
papers using different grids report different IBS values for the same model.

**Do not read it when.** The model does not produce survival probabilities at
all — a risk-only model gets `NA` here, by design, because inventing a
distribution is worse than admitting there is none.

## Calibration: is the number right?

**Question.** When the model says S(t) = 0.8, do 8 out of 10 such patients
really survive past `t`?

```{r calibration}
calibration <- surv_calibration_curves(
  data$time, data$status, survival, time_points
)
calibration$summary
```

Four numbers, one per time point, all from the same grouped comparison
(groups are formed from the *predictions*, never from the outcome):

* **ICI** — the patient-weighted mean absolute gap between prediction and the
  group Kaplan-Meier estimate. Small everywhere = calibrated.
* **CITL** — the group-size-weighted mean *signed* gap. Negative = predictions
  run high. This is the "calibration-in-the-large" a paper reports first.
* **E50 / E90** — the median and 90th percentile of the patient-level absolute
  error. A large ICI with a small E50 means one or two groups are badly off;
  small E50 with a large E90 means a tail of patients is badly off.

```{r calib-plot, fig.cap = "Calibration curves at the three horizons."}
plot_surv_calibration(calibration)
```

**Reading.** There is no absolute "good" ICI; compare models, and compare the
validation and external cohorts — a model calibrated at home and off abroad is
the classic external-validation finding.

The slope and intercept answer the same question with two parameters on the
complementary log-log scale: `slope = 1, intercept = 0` is perfect; below 1 is
over-confident, above 1 is timid.

```{r slope}
surv_calibration_slope(data$time, data$status, survival[, 2], time_point = 6)
```

**Do not read the coefficients when.** Fewer than ~20 patients, fewer than 5
cases or 5 controls at the horizon: the package returns `NA` with a message.
And even past that floor, read `n` and `events` first — a slope from 60
patients is noise wearing a suit.

## Risk strata and the log-rank test

**Question.** If we split the cohort by predicted risk, do the curves
separate? This is the figure prediction papers lead with.

```{r strata, fig.cap = "Kaplan-Meier by risk tercile, log-rank p in the caption."}
frame <- prepared
frame$group <- surv_risk_groups(risk, k = 3)
plot_surv_km(frame, spec, group = "group", logrank = TRUE)
```

**Reading.** Curves should separate and stay ordered (lowest risk on top).
The log-rank p-value tests whether the separation is larger than chance.

**Do not read it when.** You want a clinical threshold. The strata are
sample-relative terciles, not decision boundaries — a patient at the Q2/Q3
border is not a treatment decision. And a significant log-rank p-value says
the strata differ, not that the model is calibrated: a shifted model
separates perfectly and is still wrong. The calibration section is the one
that answers "is the number right".

## Decision curves

**Question.** If we treat patients above threshold `p`, does acting on the
model beat treating everybody and beat treating nobody?

```{r dca, fig.cap = "Decision curves at the three horizons."}
dca <- surv_dca_curves(data$time, data$status, survival, time_points)
plot_surv_dca(dca)
```

**Reading.** Net benefit at threshold `p` is (true positives − false
positives × p/(1−p)) / n. Compare the model curve with the treat-all curve at
the thresholds a clinic would actually use: the model wins wherever it sits
above treat-all. Censored patients are weighted by the censoring survival, so
loss to follow-up is not silently counted as "no event".

**Do not read it when.** The threshold range includes values no clinic would
ever use; the y axis is clipped for exactly this reason, and the full curve
data are in `surv_dca_curves()`'s table.

## What to report, on one page

| Question | Metric | Good | Read with care |
|---|---|---|---|
| Who is sicker (overall) | `cindex`, `uno_c` | 0.7+ | differing censoring distributions |
| Who is sicker by horizon | `auc_t`, `auc_uno_t` | 0.7+ | small `n_case`/`n_control` |
| Is S(t) close to the truth | `brier_t`, `ibs` | beats the KM baseline | grid dependence of `ibs` |
| Is the number right | `ici`, `citl`, `e50`, `e90` | small; citl near 0 | group smoothing, sample size |
| Slope and intercept | `calib_slope`, `calib_intercept` | 1 and 0 | < 100 patients: skip |
| Does it change decisions | `dca` | above treat-all in the clinical range | threshold choice |
| Do strata separate | stratified KM + log-rank | ordered separation | presentation only, not thresholds |
